transcript.text: Australia's mushroom murderer was hoping her conviction would be quashed. Now she faces a prospect of dying in prison. Here's what we know. Erin Patterson killed three of her relatives after serving them a meal containing toxic death cat mushrooms. She was sentenced to life in prison last year. She appealed, challenging some of the evidence that was and wasn't allowed in the trial, as well as her cross-examination and the way the jury was held during deliberations. The judges dismissed Patterson's appeal. her conviction stands. They did, however, agree with the prosecution's appeal that her life sentence with a parole period after 33 years was wrong. The judges said her crimes were extraordinarily cold and calculated, so shocking she should never be allowed freedom. Her only legal option now is to ask Australia's High Court to look at her case.

sources.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson likely to die in jail after failed appeal - ABC News
sources.text: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson likely to die in jail after failed appeal By court reporter Kristian Silva and Tim Callanan Topic: Courts Posted Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 10:13am Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 10:13am Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 10:13am , updated Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 3:53pm Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 3:53pm Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 3:53pm Erin Patterson was resentenced to life in prison without parole. ( NewsWire: Jason Edwards ) In short: Victoria's highest court has removed the possibility of parole for jailed triple murderer Erin Patterson. The court also rejected Patterson's appeal against her convictions for killing her relatives with a beef Wellington meal laced with death cap mushrooms. What's next? It is unclear whether Patterson's legal team will mount a challenge in the High Court. abc.net.au/news/erin-patterson-loses-mushroom-murder-convictions-appeal/107326714 Link copied Share Share article Erin Patterson will die in prison, after Victoria's highest court stripped the mushroom killer of a chance of parole and labelled her crimes "extraordinarily cold and calculated". In its judgment, published in full this afternoon, Victoria's Court of Appeal increased Patterson's sentence for poisoning her relatives and dismissed all grounds of her appeal. Patterson was last year sentenced to life in prison with a non-parole period of 33 years for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson, along with the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian. The group were poisoned with death cap mushrooms that Patterson had baked into beef Wellingtons, which she served at a lunch in 2023. Today, appeal judges Stephen McLeish, Lesley Taylor and Peter Kidd decided to remove the non-parole period altogether, meaning Patterson's sentence will expire upon death. Loading... “This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms," the judges wrote. " On any view, these were heinous crimes. " They described Patterson's crime as a case "of such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period". Few killers in Australia are serving life sentences with no parole. Some include Martin Bryant, who carried out the Port Arthur massacre, Snowtown killers John Bunting and Robert Wagner, and serial murderer Peter Dupas. It is unclear whether Patterson's legal team will mount a challenge in the High Court. ( ABC News: Anita Lester ) Justice McLeish described Patterson's actions as "carefully planned and deliberate". "The applicant's intent to murder all four victims was sustained for nearly three weeks from when she invited them to lunch, through to preparing and serving the poisoned meal and then throughout the protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted," he said. Patterson, who watched the proceedings on a video link, sat back in her seat and appeared to stare blankly when the decision was announced. She is being held in the maximum security wing of the Dame Phyllis Frost women's prison. Erin Patterson's appeal rejected : Look back on how today's hearing unfolded in our blog. Outside the court, prosecutors, police investigators and supporters of Patterson's ex-husband Simon Patterson grinned broadly. It is unclear whether her legal team will mount a challenge in the High Court of Australia. In August, the prosecution argued Patterson's offending was in the "worst category" of murders, and called for the non-parole period to be scrapped. They also submitted the sentencing judge Christopher Beale erred by finding Patterson was likely to be held in solitary confinement "for years to come" because of her notoriety. Patterson left with few legal avenues The three judges of the appeal court also dismissed the 52-year-old's appeal against her convictions. In Patterson's conviction appeal, her lawyers argued her trial last year was compromised by what they described as a "catastrophic" arrangement, where members of the jury were in the same hotel as police and prosecutors . The appeal judges said the jury setup "offered fertile grounds for speculation" but there was no reason to believe a miscarriage of justice occurred. Patterson's other six appeal grounds were also unsuccessful. More on Erin Patterson 'She's no dope': Who is the host of Australia's most infamous lunch? Topic: Courts Patterson's failed appeal leaves few legal avenues for the mushroom killer Topic: Explainer How a recipe of 'ultimate indulgence' became central to a murder plot Topic: Courts Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson barred from selling Leongatha home Topic: Courts Patterson's lawyers argued mobile cell towers and iNaturalist website evidence should not have been put to the jury, however the judges found the evidence was relevant to the prosecution's circumstantial case. They also dismissed claims the trial judge incorrectly ruled that an old SD card with mushroom photos and videos was inadmissible during the prosecution case; and that critical Facebook messages Patterson had written about her extended family should have been excluded. The defence had accused senior prosecutor Nanette Rogers SC of conducting an "unfair and oppressive" cross-examination of Patterson in the witness box. The appeal judges said Dr Rogers was "ably and fairly discharging her obligations" under the legal rule of Browne v Dunn, which require allegations to be put directly to a person under cross-examination. While the court found Dr Rogers's closing address had "some blemishes", it was not unfair. Finally, the court rejected claims the prosecution changed its case by telling the jury there was no motive, but then implied one existed by the end of the trial. The decision to reject Patterson's appeal leaves her with few legal options , including appealing to the High Court. Loading...
